stem: Meera's grandmother follows a purely lunar calendar in which each month begins with a new Moon, and 12 such lunar months make one lunar year of about 354 days. Meera notices that a festival fixed to a particular lunar month falls in winter one year but, after several years, falls in the rainy season. Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.text: The Moon's phases change randomly, so no calendar based on them can ever repeat in a regular way.
Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar year ends earlier and the months drift through the seasons.
The seasons themselves become a little shorter each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
The Moon takes exactly 30 days to complete its phases, which matches the seasonal year, so any mismatch must be due to counting errors.

teacher.key_rationale: A lunar year of 12 lunar months is about 354 days, roughly 11 days shorter than the ~365-day seasonal (solar) year. Each lunar year therefore finishes earlier relative to the seasons, so the same lunar month shifts earlier each year and gradually moves through all seasons. Option B states this. A is wrong because lunar phases are regular; C is wrong because the seasonal cycle is essentially fixed by Earth's orbit; D is wrong because the lunar cycle (~29.5 days) does not match the solar year.
